style_context: Pottery tools, clay bodies, hand-building methods, potter's wheels, kilns, and ceramic materials

images.description: Realistic pottery studio worktable arranged for safe use with a clean apron, tied-back hair, sponge and bucket for wet cleanup, neatly stored trimming and carving tools with tips pointed safely away, clay scraps contained, clear walkway, and a kiln in the background with a marked safety zone. Add only a few short instructional callouts such as wet cleanup, safe tool storage, tied-back hair, and clear kiln area. No logos, no branding, no decorative title.
images.value: Shows the physical layout of safe pottery habits, tool placement, and kiln clearance in one view — studio setup details are easier to learn visually than from a verbal list

images.description: Clean side-by-side educational diagram of two clay body samples in cutaway view. Left sample is hand-building clay with slightly rougher groggy texture and a labeled tall sculptural form beside it. Right sample is smoother wheel-throwing clay beside a centered cylinder on a pottery wheel. Use only short labels like hand-building, throwing, grog, smooth, and stronger support. Keep layout simple and text minimal.
images.value: Side-by-side visual comparison of coarse hand-building clay versus smoother throwing clay with matching use cases — texture and fit-for-purpose differences are hard to grasp from words alone

images.description: Simple three-column diagram of a kick wheel, treadle wheel, and electric potter's wheel, each shown from the side with the wheel head, power source, and motion path clearly visible. Show a foot kicking the flywheel on the kick wheel, a pumping treadle on the treadle wheel, and a motor with pedal control on the electric wheel. Use only short horizontal labels for the three types and a few small motion arrows.
images.value: Shows how motion is created and transferred differently in kick, treadle, and electric wheels — mechanical relationships are much clearer in a visual comparison

images.description: Illustrated overhead view of two pottery concept sketches on white paper. One sketch is a historical amphora with simple labels for rim, neck, shoulder, belly, and foot. The second is a modern Scout-designed mug or vase concept with notes pointing to handle shape, base stability, and decoration zone. Keep labels short and clean, no branding, no decorative title.
images.value: Shows how pottery forms are broken into design parts like rim, shoulder, and foot on both a historical and original sketch — planning structure is easier to understand visually than through description alone

images.description: Three-panel instructional diagram showing the main hand-building methods. Panel one shows flat slabs being joined into a cup or box form. Panel two shows coils stacked into a pot. Panel three shows hands pinching open a small clay bowl. Clean white background, minimal short labels only: slab, coil, pinch. No decorative text.
images.value: Shows the distinct starting shapes and hand motions for slab, coil, and pinch construction side by side — procedural differences are immediately clearer visually

images.description: Four-panel educational illustration comparing major ceramic products beyond craft pottery: ceramic floor tile, a white sink or toilet fixture, spark plugs, and a dense technical ceramic component, with a handmade mug included for scale and comparison. Use only tiny short labels under each object, simple neutral background, no branding or title text.
images.value: Shows how widely ceramic products differ in shape and purpose across household and technical uses — the visual range of non-pottery ceramics is much easier to grasp by sight

images.description: Realistic outdoor kiln yard scene at a craft school showing four distinct kiln types in one training view: an electric kiln, a gas kiln, a larger wood or soda kiln structure, and a small raku setup. Include an adult guide and a Scout-aged visitor in clean non-messy clothes observing from a safe distance. Add a few short callouts naming each kiln type and marking the safe viewing area. No logos, no organizational text.
images.value: Shows the real scale and visual differences among electric, gas, wood or soda, and raku kilns in one shared setting — comparing kiln types in place is difficult to teach with text alone
